articles.title: Inside France: Police raids, politicians' private lives and protest banners expo
articles.text:
Inside France: Police raids, politicians' private lives and protest banners expo
Advertisement
Inside France
Inside France: Police raids, politicians' private lives and protest banners expo
Emma Pearson - emma.pearson@thelocal.com
Published: 21 Nov, 2026 CET.
Updated: Sat 21 Nov 2026 11:51 CET
Add a comment
A protester holds a placard reading "Bold, united youth sheds light on the dark corners" at a protest in Nantes, western France on October 24, 2026. Photo by Guillaume Saligot / AFP
Add The Local as a preferred source
From the police raids at a political party's HQ to the romantic lives of French public figures, via a museum appeal for France's best protest slogans, here's what we have been talking about in France this week.
Inside France is editor Emma Pearson's weekly look at some of the news, talking points and gossip in France that you might not have heard about. It’s published each Saturday and members can receive it directly to their inbox, by going to their newsletter preferences or adding their email to the sign-up box in this article.
French police were once again raiding the headquarters of Marine Le Pen's Rassemblement National this week, this time investigating suspicions that a 'mole' inside the Interior Ministry provided secret information to the party about ongoing investigations.
The long-running embezzlement case about against Le Pen and senior party leadership ended last year with a raft of convictions, but there are other investigations ongoing.
Advertisement
The European Public Prosecutor’s Office said in June they were conducting searches in France and other countries into alleged misappropriation of EU funds by a defunct far-right group in the European parliament, which included RN politicians.
Meanwhile EU prosecutors are also investigating after anti-graft association AC!! Anti-Corruption alleged that funds held by members of the RN in their capacity as MEPs were used “for purposes other than those for which they were allocated”.
Le Monde newspaper said evidence had emerged “suggesting that RN was benefiting from confidential information about judicial investigations targeting the party, coming from at least one senior official at the interior ministry, who has since been reassigned but remains a high-ranking civil servant”.
French media immediately launched a hunt for la taupe (the mole), suspected of passing on the information.
Don't miss our journalists' daily news roundup from France
While these are undoubtedly serious allegations, they reminded me of French TV series Au Service de la France, from which I learned the word taupe from an episode in which the French intelligence agency discovers that it has a mole.
I always recommend that series to anyone interested in France, because it's a great piece of French self-parody. It also contains this, perhaps the greatest piece of commentary ever on the cultural chasm between France and the US.
The idea that all French politicians have mistresses and no-one cares is no longer quite so set in stone as it was in the 1960s, while the cosy collaboration between politics and media that led to French journalists hushing up scandals up to and including a president's secret love child is a thing of the past.
In fact, just this week the French state broadcaster found itself in hot water after it introduced a guest, the head of a feminist campaign group, by announcing that she is in a relationship with a senior executive at the TV Channel. France Télévisions said it was required to do this by a new code on transparency, but Anne-Cecile Mailfert has received the support of several high-profile politicians, emphasising her right to a private life.
But while the media might be governed by the code on transparency, discussion of the private lives of the leading 2027 presidential candidates remains mostly off-limits within French media.
Advertisement
Talking France
On the Talking France podcast we discuss French citizenship changes and what they say about today's political climate, as well as the presidential candidates' policies for rural France and the best seasonal specialities in France in November.
We also discuss the case of the €8,000 libido - aka why you shouldn't argue with a French ticket inspector.
Listen here.
The kids are . . . going to be in a museum
As regular readers will know, I've very much enjoyed the wide range of smart, witty, erudite, silly and sometimes rude banners glimpsed on the lycée protests - if writing cool political slogans was in the Olympics, French kids would be world champions.
READ ALSO: Bac to f**k: Understanding French lycées protest signs
And apparently I'm not the only one - the Musée de l'histoire vivant (living history museum) in Montreuil has put out a call for people to send in their banners, with a view to forming an exhibition.
It's tough to pick just one, but I think the Brets crisps banner remains my favourite so far, while the ones written in Latin by the kids at Paris' posh Lycée Henri IV were, for me, a bit too try-hard.
New Brets crisps spotted at today's protests - 'burning bin' and 'tear-gassed kids' flavours
[image or embed]
— Emma Pearson ( @emmapearson.bsky.social) 5 November 2026 at 18:18
Advertisement
Global city
And while news from the 2027 election campaign trail remains quite grim for foreigners in France; harsh anti-immigration measures in a lot of the manifestos and the increasing chance of a Marine Le Pen v Jean-Luc Mélenchon second round (which all polling projects that Le Pen would win handily), let's take a moment to appreciate people who don't indulge in immigrant bashing.
Billboard in Paris from City Hall, reading 'One Parisian in 4 was born abroad'. Photo: The Local
Paris city hall regularly runs these kinds of campaigns celebrating its foreign-born residents and their contribution to the city and has long adopted the tag 'Paris, ville-monde' saying: "Paris is a global city. It is an open city, enriched by the diversity of the people who bring it to life, th

articles.title: Do you need a financial advisor when living in France?
articles.text:
Do you need a financial advisor when living in France?
Presented By Arisaig Wealth Management
Do you need a financial advisor when living in France?
Financial planning often takes a back seat when you move abroad as you get to grips with everyday life. It's easy to let years pass without taking a proper look at your finances. But a lot can change in that time, and hoping everything will work out can mean missing opportunities.
Published: Thu 29 Oct 2026 11:36 CEST
Photo: Maurijn Pach / Pexels
You might have had a financial plan in your home country, or the last country you lived in. Left on autopilot, it may not suit your current circumstances, country of residence, tax position, or long-term plans.
Not everyone living abroad has a financial advisor, or even needs one. Some people might manage their investments, pensions, and savings themselves, while others might have worked with an advisor in the past but no longer have an active relationship.
The first question is whether your current financial arrangements suit your life today. It could be that your income, family situation, retirement plans, risk tolerance, and expected investment timeframe have changed and it’s time to rethink your original plan.
Want to make sure your finances still work for you? Find out how Arisaig Wealth can help.
Take stock of what you have
Your country of residence matters, especially if it’s not your home country. An investment or pension arrangement that worked for you while living in one country may not make financial sense after you move to the EU.
Tax and reporting rules can also vastly differ between countries. It's important to understand how your investments, pensions, and other assets are treated in your current country of tax residence rather than assuming the rules from your home or previous country still apply.
If you're not sure where to start, begin by taking an inventory of what you actually own. Identify any investments, pensions, and other financial products–such as savings accounts, investment funds, shares, or insurance-based products–where they are and how they are set up.
Photo: Arisaig Wealth Management
Note what you're paying, from product charges and investment-management fees to any other related ongoing costs. You may find that older products in particular have charging structures that aren't instantly obvious, so read and then re-read the fine print.
Once you've got your head around everything, find out how flexible your existing arrangements are. Check whether you can change investments, withdraw contributions, transfer the product, or change beneficiaries where relevant.
It’s especially important to understand the terms of older products, as some may have restrictions or penalties for changes.
Time for a financial health check? Find out how Arisaig Wealth can help.
Review your investment strategy as a whole, not just individual products. Ask yourself: ‘Does the overall portfolio still match my attitude to risk, timeframe and objectives?’ and ‘Is the portfolio appropriately diversified?’
A financial planner, such as Arisaig Wealth, can help you create a structured financial plan designed around milestones, changes, and uncertainties.
Look at the bigger picture
Existing arrangements may still be useful, and older or less flexible ones can sometimes remain part of a wider financial plan. Changing or replacing them can be tricky, but understanding how they work alongside your other assets can make planning easier.
Cross-border finances add yet another layer of complexity. For instance, you may have a pension in one country, investments in another, and income in your new country. Look at how everything works together, rather than reviewing each in isolation.
Then there's currency. You may be earning in Euros while holding investments or expecting future retirement income in US dollars, pounds, or another currency. That can create currency risk that you should take into account in your overall plan.
Arisaig Wealth provides integrated, objectives-based financial planning that reflects your global situation, helping you make informed decisions with confidence.
Plan for your next move
If another international move is on the cards, factor it into any planning too. Moving countries can affect taxation, reporting requirements, and even access to certain investments. Reviewing arrangements before relocating can help you spot potential problems early on.
If all this sounds like a lot to handle without expert support, make sure to work with a financial advisor who knows their way around cross-border finances. Things can get complicated when your pension is in one country, your investments are in another, and you're paying tax somewhere else entirely. This is where Arisaig Wealth can help, offering independent advice for expatriates and international professionals.
The aim isn't necessarily to find new financial products. It's to determine whether your current arrangements still support your goals and make sense for your circumstances.
Ready to take control of your finances? Contact Arisaig Wealth to find out how their team can help.

articles.title: Everything that changes in France in December 2026
articles.text:
Everything that changes in France in December 2026
Advertisement
What changes in France
Members only
Everything that changes in France in December 2026
Emma Albright - emma.albright@thelocal.com
Published: 20 Nov, 2026 CET.
Updated: Fri 20 Nov 2026 08:39 CET
Add a comment
A Christmas market in downtown Nantes on December 22nd, 2025. (Photo by Loic VENANCE / AFP)
Add The Local as a preferred source
From a rise in gas prices to the opening of ski resorts and the start of the Christmas holidays, here's what changes in December 2026.
Strikes
Professional firefighters (sapeurs-pompiers professionnels) are planning a nationwide mobilisation on Friday, December 4th.
The inter-union group representing fire and rescue service employees is calling on firefighters to leave their helmets outside préfectures across France.
We keep our strike calendar up to date as soon we know when a strike has been planned here.
Protests?
The Gilet Jaunes have held protests on consecutive Saturdays ever since October 17th, and say they intend to continue. Although turnout has fallen in recent weeks, Saturday protests in bigger cities are still attracting thousands of people, with tight policing.
Budget?
The end of the year marks the final deadline for parliament to agree the 2027 Budget, with votes normally taking place in both houses by mid-December at the latest.
Parliament has until December 17th to adopt it, with overall budget adoption deadlines running through December 31st, 2026.
Advertisement
This year, it appears unlikely that prime minister Sébastien Lecornu will be able to pass his budget through a deadlocked parliament, although a last-minute deal is always possible. If he cannot pass it, he will have to resort to constitutional powers which open him up to a vote of no confidence.
In short - expect budget-related shenanigans in December, and possibly the fall of (another) French government.
Gas prices
The benchmark price of gas (prix repère de vente du gaz) will increase by 5.8 percent in December, according to the Commission de régulation de l'énergie (CRE).
The benchmark price is published monthly and is used by consumers to compare gas offers from suppliers. It is not a compulsory tariff - the actual amount customers pay depends on their contract and supplier.
READ MORE: French gas prices to rise for a fourth month in a row in December
Ski resorts open
While some of the high-altitude resorts opened during the last week of November, most French ski resorts will not open until mid-to-late December, subject to appropriate weather conditions.
Find out what's changing in France with our weekly and monthly outlook
New restrictions on bicycles aboard some trains
From December 13th, certain bicycles will no longer be permitted aboard TGV and Intercités services. The change concerns particular types of bicycles.
The new rules specifically ban: fatbikes, which have particularly wide tyres, bicycles with more than two wheels, bicycles longer than 185cm or with tyres wider than 6cm, gyropodes and hoverboards.
The restrictions apply to TGV INOUI and Intercités trains. Passengers who breach the baggage rules can face a fine of €50 per non-compliant item, rising to €150.
French film screenings
Lost in Frenchlation - the cinema club that screens French films with English subtitles - has several screenings in store for December in Paris. This month also includes some Christmas classics.
READ MORE: French films with English subtitles to watch in December 2026
Christmas bonus
Each year, France gives certain households the Prime de Nöel, an end-of-year bonus, also known as the Christmas bonus, to be paid out on December 15th.
Advertisement
It is reserved for low-income households and those who qualify for the government's top-up benefit, RSA. More info here.
Sending Christmas gifts
If you are planning to send Christmas presents by post, it is best to get them on their way early. The run-up to Christmas is one of the busiest periods for postal services, and delays are more likely as December progresses.
For 2026, La Poste recommends sending standard parcels within mainland France around mid-December at the latest. Its general guidance suggests allowing extra time for overseas destinations, ideally sending international parcels at the beginning of December or earlier.
FedEx has published its 2026 Christmas deadlines. For US deliveries by December 24th, it recommends sending by December 17th using International Priority, or December 13th using International Economy.
Fête des Lumières
Between Friday, December 5th, and Monday, December 8th, visitors to the south-eastern city of Lyon are invited to enjoy enchanting walks in an ever-changing sea of light and sound - including large projections over the city’s most beautiful monuments. You’ll find displays over the facades of major landmarks and scattered around the city as you walk (perhaps with a vin chaud in hand).
Advertisement
Christmas markets
Most French Christmas markets start in late November and run either until the end of December or early January.
READ ALSO: 10 of the best Christmas markets to visit in France this year
Property taxes
The deadline to pay the taxe d'habitation on second homes (résidences secondaires) is December 15th for taxpayers not using online payment. Those paying online have until December 20th at midnight.
This tax was abolished for main residences in 2023 but remains applicable to second homes.
READ ALSO: Taxe foncière: How to challenge your 2026 French property tax bills
School holidays begin
Schoolchildren across France will have time off from Saturday, December 19th to Monday, January 4th for the Christmas break. There is often heavy traffic on the roads the evening before the start of the school holidays and over that weekend, so keep this in mind when making your travel plans.
Parcoursup for university applications
The online platform, Parcoursup, for pre-registration for the first year of higher education opens on December 17, 2026.
Chris

articles.title: French expression of the day: Faire machine arrière
articles.text:
French expression of the day: Faire machine arrière
Advertisement
French Word of the Day
Members only
French expression of the day: Faire machine arrière
The Local France - news@thelocal.fr
Published: 20 Nov, 2026 CET.
Updated: Sat 21 Nov 2026 09:42 CET
Add a comment
Photo: Annie Spratt/Unsplash/ Nicolas Raymond
Add The Local as a preferred source
If you find yourself irresolute, wavering and wobbling, you could be about to do this.
Why do I need to know faire machine arrière?
A good French expression to know if you're ever unsure about something you've already committed to.
Don't miss our journalists' daily news roundup from France
What does it mean?
Faire machine arrière, roughly pronounced fehr mah-sheen ah-ryehr (listen here), literally translates as to "make a machine go backwards". It was originally used during the 19th century in a very literal sense to describe the process of making a steam engine or a propeller turn the other way.
Today the expression is mostly used to in a figurative sense to describe human acts of backpedalling or retreat. It's frequently used about politicians who change their minds or go back on their promises.
Another expression you could use in the same way is faire marche arrière (backing up), rétropedalage (backpedalling), renoncer (abandon) or faire demi-tour (make a U-turn).
Advertisement
So if you were a French political commentator and strike action was looming, you might be asking yourself: le gouvernement fera-t-il machine arrière? - Will the government make a U-turn?
Use it like this
Face aux critiques, le maire a décidé de faire machine arrière. - Faced with criticism, the mayor decided to backpedal.
L'entreprise a fait machine arrière après la réaction négative de ses clients. - The company backtracked after the negative reaction from its customers.
Je pensais déménager à Lyon, mais j'ai fait machine arrière. - I was thinking of moving to Lyon, but I changed my mind.

Host Ben McPartland is joined by The Local France's Emma Pearson and Emma Albright, politics expert John Lichfield and Brittany-based journalist Katy Wright with all the latest news from France.
You can find the Talking France podcast on Spotify, Apple or the French platform  Deezer or on  World Radio Paris. You can download it here or listen to the full episode on the link below.
We begin with a topic that could have a massive impact on the lives of some foreigners in France - changes to French citizenship rules. But what's really going on here? And why was the announcement slipped out so quietly?
Stay informed with our essential Talking France newsletter

articles.title: Two Brits charged over €16m French château fraud
articles.text:
Two Brits charged over €16m French château fraud
Advertisement
Crime
Two Brits charged over €16m French château fraud
Emma Pearson - emma.pearson@thelocal.com
Published: 13 Nov, 2026 CET.
Updated: Sat 21 Nov 2026 08:14 CET
Add a comment
A screenshot from the brochure of the chateau development. Image: Halcyon
Add The Local as a preferred source
Two British businessmen have been formally charged over a suspected fraud of €16 million centred on a château in south-west France.
Back in May, after a lengthy investigation into potential fraud and money laundering, a British businessman was arrested in Spain and extradited back to France.
Now, the man and his business partner have been charged (mis en examen) in France in relation to the case, after a court hearing in Bordeaux in early November.
Former police officer Robin Barrasford, 56, was charged with 'fraud and money laundering by an organised group'. He has been released on bail of €250,000 and has been banned from leaving French territory.
Advertisement
His business partner Alan Bird, 79, was also charged and released on a bail bond of €800,000 - his bail conditions state that he can only leave France for trips to the UK and back.
Both deny the charges. Their lawyer Julien Plouton told the court that they intend to argue that the scheme was a good faith business enterprise that ended in “a commercial collapse linked to the economic climate”.
The alleged fraud centres on a château in Noth, near Limoges in south-west France, which the two Brits bought for €2.5 million.
They created brochures showing a planned luxury golf and spa retreat - the Halcyon Retreat and Golf Spa - complete with private chalets in the woods surrounding the château, and began advertising for investors, promising them free use of the chalets as well as a hefty profit on their investments in the luxury development.
Stay ahead of the news on buying & owning property in France
But according to the financial crimes unit in Limoges, work never even began on the site and instead the cash from investors - estimated to be around €16 million - was funnelled into a network of offshore bank accounts.
The Local has spoken to several people who invested their life savings in the project, hoping for a retirement home or a property investment, and were left with nothing.

How and when to send Christmas presents from France in 2026
Advertisement
Living in France
Members only
How and when to send Christmas presents from France in 2026
The Local France - news@thelocal.fr
Published: 28 Nov, 2022 CET.
Updated: Fri 20 Nov 2026 17:19 CET
1 comment
Photo by Christophe ARCHAMBAULT / AFP
Add The Local as a preferred source
If you want to send Christmas presents to friends and family overseas you need to know the deadline dates and how to avoid being hit with extra charges - here's are the deadlines for 2026.
Deadlines
First things first, you need to make sure your parcel arrives in time for Christmas, which means sending it before the deadline.
France's postal service, La Poste, has published its recommended last posting dates for Christmas 2026. However, the deadlines vary considerably depending on where you are sending your parcel and which delivery service you use.
Get our essential newsletter for Britons living in and moving to Europe
Sending parcels within France
If you are sending a Christmas parcel within mainland France, La Poste's Colissimo service has the following recommended last posting dates for delivery before Christmas:
December 21st for a standard two-day delivery (J+2).
December 22nd for a next-day delivery (J+1).
December 23rd for a same-day delivery service (J).
These are the dates published in Colissimo's 2026 Christmas calendar. It is still advisable to send parcels earlier, particularly during the busy Christmas period.
Advertisement
In Europe
If you are sending a parcel to another European country, the deadline depends on the destination. The recommended last posting dates from mainland France are:
December 15th - Bulgaria, Cyprus, Estonia, Greece, Latvia, Norway and Slovenia.
December 16th - the US, Czech Republic, Spanish and Portuguese islands (e.g. Tenerife and Madeira), Finland, Hungary, Ireland, Lithuania, Malta, Poland, Romania and Slovakia.
December 17th - Austria, Switzerland, Denmark, Portugal, Croatia, Iceland, Italy, the Netherlands and Sweden.
December 18th - Germany, Belgium, Luxembourg, mainland Spain and the UK.
Advertisement
Outside Europe
For destinations outside Europe, the deadlines are:
December 11th - Canada, China, Japan, South Korea, Thailand, Hong Kong, Singapore and Vietnam.
December 9th - most other international destinations (listed as the 'rest of the world' by Colissimo).
For French overseas territories, the deadlines are:
December 9th - New Caledonia, French Polynesia, Saint-Pierre-et-Miquelon and Saint-Martin.
December 11th - Mayotte and French Guiana.
December 15th - Guadeloupe, Martinique and Réunion.
Full list here.
What about private couriers?
Private couriers such as FedEx and Chronopost have their own Christmas delivery deadlines. For FedEx, parcels sent to Europe should generally be posted by December 21st at the latest, while those sent to the US should be sent by December 17th, depending on the service chosen.
Check the FedEx 2026 Christmas delivery calendar for full deadlines by destination and service.
If you are ordering gifts online, remember that retailers also have their own last ordering dates for guaranteed Christmas delivery.
Advertisement
Last-minute gift sending?
If you are running out of time, Chronopost - La Poste's express delivery service may be a good solution.
Chronopost offers next-day delivery through certain services, provided you drop off your parcel before the relevant cut-off time. Its Chrono 13 service also offers delivery before 1pm on the next working day in eligible areas.
This can be useful for last-minute Christmas presents, although availability, delivery times and cut-off hours depend on the destination and the service selected. Check with your local post office or Chronopost before sending.
Fees and customs declarations
If you are sending parcels to another EU country, the process is generally straightforward - you simply pay the delivery cost and make sure your parcel is sent before the deadline. You can calculate the cost of sending a parcel through La Poste's website.
If, however, you are sending to a country outside the EU, you will generally need to complete a customs declaration explaining what is inside your parcel, its value and whether it is a gift.
Customs rules vary depending on the destination. You may also need to pay customs duties or import taxes, depending on the contents and value of your parcel, as well as the rules in the receiving country.
READ ALSO: What you should know about sending packages to and from France at Christmas
Banned items
And there are some items that are banned from the post - if you're sending parcels to the US be aware that you cannot send alcohol through the mail as a private individual, so don't try to ship some nice French wine or a bottle of your local liqueur.
Most countries ban firearms and fireworks, not unreasonably, although be aware that this includes items like sparklers.
Sending food and plants is also often restricted, with countries including Canada and Australia having strict rules and most other countries imposing restrictions on what you can send.
This also applies the other way and France bans any foodstuffs containing animal products (eg chocolate) sent from outside the EU.
The precise rules depend on the destination and the contents of your parcel, so check La Poste's country-specific shipping guidance before packing your gifts.
